lead: A dimensionless number is a ratio of two forces or energies in a flow, or the square root of such a ratio. It has no units. When one such ratio is large, that force controls the flow. Engineers use these numbers to compare pipe flows, ship waves, droplets and aircraft without carrying units. The five common groups are Reynolds, Froude, Euler, Weber and Mach. Each answers a simple question: is inertia stronger than viscosity, gravity, pressure, surface tension or compressibility? The same numbers decide model tests, so a small model can predict a full-size machine.
prereq: You need 5.6 for where dimensionless groups come from and 5.5 for units.

blocks.text: A flow has several forces acting at once. Inertia is the tendency of moving fluid to keep going. Pick two forces. Divide one by the other. Both have the unit newton, so the newtons cancel. The result is a pure number. Its name records which pair you divided. A large value means the force on top is strong. A small value means the force below is strong. This is the whole habit behind dimensionless numbers.

Table 5.7.1 lists the five groups used in this unit. The symbols are: ρ is density in kg/m³; V is a representative speed in m/s; D is a pipe or sphere diameter in m; L is a length in m, such as plate length, channel depth or droplet diameter; μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; ν = μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity in m²/s; g is gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s²; Δp is a pressure difference in Pa; σ is surface tension in N/m; c is the speed of sound in the fluid in m/s.

head: Group
Formula
Ratio
What a large value means
rows: viscosity is too weak to smooth the flow; turbulence is likely
gravity waves are slow compared with the flow; flow is supercritical
pressure change is large compared with the moving fluid's kinetic energy
surface tension cannot hold the surface together; droplets break up
compressibility changes density; shock waves are possible

blocks.text: The formulas assume one chosen V and one chosen L. Change the length, and the number changes. State your length choice in every answer.

In a pipe, use the inside diameter for D. Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. Re below about 2000 gives laminar flow. Re above about 4000 gives turbulent flow. Between them the flow is transitional. This is why honey and water behave differently in the same tube: honey has high μ, so its Re is low. Pipe friction uses Re; see Unit 4, Viscous Flow Through Pipes.

Froude number needs a free surface. L is the hydraulic depth, area ÷ top width; for a simple rectangular channel it is the water depth. Fr < 1 is subcritical. Small waves travel faster than the flow, so the flow can feel a downstream control. Fr = 1 is critical. Fr > 1 is supercritical. A hydraulic jump can form.

Euler number compares a measured pressure drop with the dynamic pressure ½ρV². A valve with large Eu has a large loss. Weber number matters when surface tension is not negligible: droplets, bubbles and thin jets. Mach number compares flow speed with sound speed c in the gas. Below Ma ≈ 0.3, density changes are small and the flow is treated as incompressible. Above that, use compressible flow relations; see Unit 3, Fluid Dynamics and Flow Measurement. Heat transfer has its own groups, such as Nusselt and Prandtl; they are defined in a later subject, not derived here.

sections.h3: A short procedure for any problem

items: List every variable with its unit.
Choose the length that matches the body: diameter for a pipe or sphere, chord for an aerofoil, distance x for a flat plate, hydraulic depth for an open channel.
Check the physics: is there a free surface? is surface tension present? is the gas speed above Ma 0.3? Then pick Fr, We or Ma.
Compute the number. Cancel the units. State the result as a pure number.

blocks.text: Pump specific speed is another dimensionless number, but it belongs with pumps; see Unit 7, Centrifugal and Reciprocating Pumps.

figure.caption: The block diagram places each group beside the pair of forces it divides. Reynolds number is the first branch because the worked example computes it first.

spec.title: Force ratios behind dimensionless numbers
spec.aria: A central box labelled dimensionless groups branches to five boxes: Re, Fr, Eu, We and Ma, each with its force ratio.

examples.question: A 20 mm diameter sphere moves at V = 0.5 m/s through water with ρ = 1000 kg/m³, ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s and surface tension σ = 0.072 N/m. The pressure difference across it is measured as 200 Pa. Compute Re, We and Eu. Use D as the sphere diameter.
steps: Reynolds number: Re = VD/ν = 0.5 × 0.020 / (1.0×10⁻⁶) = 0.010 / (1.0×10⁻⁶) = 1.0×10⁴. It has no unit.
Weber number: We = ρV²D/σ = 1000 × (0.5)² × 0.020 / 0.072 = 1000 × 0.25 × 0.020 / 0.072 = 5 / 0.072 = 69.4 (rounded to one decimal). It has no unit.
Euler number: Eu = Δp/(½ρV²) = 200 / (0.5 × 1000 × 0.25) = 200 / 125 = 1.6. It has no unit.
Unit check: ρV² is in Pa; multiplying by D (m) gives Pa·m = N/m, the same unit as σ. So We = (N/m)/(N/m) is a pure number. Re is (m/s × m)/(m²/s), also unit-free. Eu is Pa/Pa.
examples.answer: Re = 1.0×10⁴, We = 69.4 and Eu = 1.6; all three are dimensionless.
examples.check:
rho = 1000.0
V = 0.5
D = 0.02
nu = 1.0e-6
sigma = 0.072
dp = 200.0
Re = V * D / nu
We = rho * V**2 * D / sigma
Eu = dp / (0.5 * rho * V**2)
print(f"{Re:.1f}")
print(f"{We:.1f}")
print(f"{Eu:.1f}")

traps: Using the wrong length in Re: diameter for a pipe or sphere, chord for an aerofoil, distance x from the leading edge for a flat plate. A different D gives a different Re.
Using Froude number in a full pipe with no free surface. Gravity waves cannot form there, so Fr does not control the flow.
Forgetting the ½ in Euler number. Some books define Eu = Δp/(ρV²); with that definition every Eu is half the value used here (the value here is twice as large).
Mixing dynamic viscosity μ in Pa·s with kinematic viscosity ν in m²/s. Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν; use the matching form.
Treating Mach 1 as the start of compressibility. Density changes matter from about Ma 0.3, well below the speed of sound.

quiz.q: Define Reynolds number. Give the formula and the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. ρ in kg/m³, V in m/s, D in m, μ in Pa·s, ν in m²/s. Re has no unit.

quiz.q: Which dimensionless number compares inertia with surface tension?
Why is Froude number used only when a free surface exists?
quiz.a: Gravity waves need a free surface. In a full pipe there is no surface wave, so the gravity-to-inertia ratio does not control the flow.

quiz.q: What does a large Euler number mean for a valve?
quiz.a: The pressure drop is large compared with the dynamic pressure ½ρV², so the valve has a large loss.

quiz.q: Water flows in a 50 mm diameter pipe at V = 2 m/s. Take ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s. Compute Re.
quiz.a: D = 0.050 m. Re = VD/ν = 2 × 0.050 / (1.0×10⁻⁶) = 1.0×10⁵. The flow is turbulent.

quiz.q: A model ship 2 m long moves at 1.5 m/s. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Compute Fr.
quiz.a: Fr = V/√(gL) = 1.5/√(9.81 × 2) = 1.5/√19.62 = 1.5/4.429 = 0.339. Fr < 1, so the model flow is subcritical.

quiz.q: A gas flow has Ma = 0.1 and Re = 50000. Which effects can you neglect in the first estimate?
quiz.a: Ma = 0.1 is below 0.3, so compressibility can be neglected and density is nearly constant. Re = 50000 is high, so viscous effects are small outside the boundary layer; do not drop viscosity inside the layer.

quiz.q: Why is it usually impossible to match both Re and Fr in one scale model test?
quiz.a: Let m mean model and p mean prototype. Re matching gives V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>p</sub> = L<sub>p</sub>/L<sub>m</sub>. Fr matching gives V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>p</sub> = √(L<sub>m</sub>/L<sub>p</sub>). If the same fluid is used, both hold together only when L<sub>m</sub> = L<sub>p</sub>, that is, the model must be full size; otherwise one group must be sacrificed or a different fluid used.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, CFD codes report Re, Ma and We per cell to choose turbulence, compressibility and multiphase models. Microfluidics uses the capillary number Ca = μV/σ, closely related to We. Biomedical devices use the Womersley number for pulsatile flow. Search for 'Reynolds number pipe transition', 'Froude number open channel', 'Weber number droplet breakup' and 'Mach number compressibility'.
